clue.text: The Kilkenny Highways ?

parts.note: the Kilkenny cats of legend fought until only their tails were left; the paths such cats tread would be their highways, while the real word means a fashion runway

explanation.surface: A question about the main roads of an Irish county town.
explanation.walkthrough: The Kilkenny cats are a proverbial pair who fought each other to the death. Read the answer as paths for cats; its usual sense is the raised runway of a fashion show.
explanation.definitionFit: Fashion models parade along narrow raised runways, and the clue imagines those runways as roads built for felines.

clue.text: A whale of a jackpot, say

indicators.note: say signals that the phrase is to be spoken, giving a word that sounds alike

parts.note: a jackpot is a big stash, a cache a lot of money

explanation.surface: Someone has won an enormous prize.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A whale of a' looks like the idiom for a huge thing, but 'A whale' is the definition: the sperm whale. 'say' signals sound: a jackpot is a big hoard, 'cache a lot'.
explanation.definitionFit: Cachalot is another name for the sperm whale, the large toothed cetacean.

clue.text: The old soldier practically asked to be shot at

definitions.meaning: a historical foot soldier armed with a round shield called a target

definitions.text: practically asked to be shot at
definitions.meaning: read as target plus -eer, one who serves as a mark for archers

explanation.definitionFit: A targeteer was a footman carrying a light shield, and the word also suggests someone who makes himself a mark to aim at.

clue.text: Bay-wrecked ship sunk deep

indicators.note: a wrecked thing is broken up, so the letters are smashed and reordered

parts.note: SS is the abbreviation for steamship

explanation.surface: A vessel wrecked in a bay sinks to the bottom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrecked' turns BAY into ABY before SS. 'deep' is a noun here, the depths of the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: The ocean depths, or any bottomless chasm, can be called the deep.

clue.text: Is not unbending respecting celestial VIP's

definitions.text: Is not unbending respecting celestial VIP's

parts.words: Is not unbending respecting celestial VIP's
parts.note: China was called the Celestial Empire; bowing low to touch the forehead to the ground before its emperor was the Chinese gesture of respect

explanation.surface: Someone refuses to stand stiffly before heavenly dignitaries.
explanation.walkthrough: 'celestial' suggests angels, but China was the Celestial Empire; its VIPs were greeted by kneeling and touching the forehead to the floor.
explanation.definitionFit: Bending low in deference to Chinese emperors gave English a word for servile submission.

clue.text: Burin more sober

definitions.meaning: a burin is an engraver's cutting tool
comparative of an adjective meaning serious or solemn

explanation.definitionFit: An engraving tool is also called by this name, and the comparative of grave means more solemn or sober.

clue.text: A canon's the fellow brings the milk

definitions.note: the clue reads 'the fellow who brings the milk', so the definition names a person by what he does

parts.note: a canon in music is a round, so a canon's is round's
a man is a fellow

explanation.surface: Someone muses that a churchman is the one who delivers the milk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'canon' looks like a clergyman, but in music a canon is a round, a song where voices enter in turn; the round's man is the deliverer on his round.
explanation.definitionFit: A tradesman who makes regular deliveries along a route, such as a milkman, is on his rounds.

clue.text: Church dignitary brought to order, with what malice !

parts.note: Ven. is the abbreviation for Venerable, the title of an archdeacon
OM is the Order of Merit, so the dignitary is given that order

explanation.surface: A senior cleric is disciplined, to someone's spiteful satisfaction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brought to order' suggests discipline, but it means VEN is followed by OM, the Order of Merit. 'with what' only joins.
explanation.definitionFit: Bitter spite or ill will is often called poisonous, so the word for poison serves for malice.

clue.text: Just what I'd be doing in the circus

definitions.text: Just what I'd be doing in the circus

indicators.note: I'd sits inside the circus, so one piece is placed within the other

parts.note: the circus ring is where the acts perform
taken as written, less the apostrophe

explanation.surface: A performer imagines their act under the big top.
explanation.walkthrough: ID inside RING, and a bareback act in the circus is exactly 'riding'.
explanation.definitionFit: A circus equestrian's act is sitting astride a horse as it canters round, so that is what one would be doing there.

clue.text: Two runs for Beds?

definitions.note: nursery talk for bed or sleep, as in 'off to ...'

indicators.note: two calls for the piece to be repeated

parts.note: a bye is a run scored in cricket without the batsman hitting the ball

explanation.surface: A request for two cricket runs on behalf of Bedfordshire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beds' looks like the abbreviation for Bedfordshire, an English county, but it is the definition: children's word for bed. A bye in cricket is a run from a ball the batsman never touched.
explanation.definitionFit: Children are told it is time for this nursery word for sleep, meaning bedtime.

clue.text: Barkis by his message did not so ecstasize Peggotty

definitions.text: Barkis by his message did not so ecstasize Peggotty

parts.words: Barkis by his message did not so ecstasize Peggotty
parts.note: in David Copperfield Barkis the carrier sends Peggotty the curt message 'Barkis is willin''; the phrase means to send into raptures, but a carrier would also literally transport her

explanation.surface: A Dickens suitor's terse proposal fails to send his beloved into raptures.
explanation.walkthrough: Barkis in Dickens's David Copperfield is a carrier who woos Peggotty with the message 'Barkis is willin''. The phrase means to transport with emotion, and a carrier's job is literally to transport.
explanation.definitionFit: To be swept off one's feet with delight is to be transported, the sense a carrier like Barkis would also serve literally.

clue.text: A tricky run by Edward took care of the Ashes

indicators.note: a tricky run is a twisty, devious one, so its letters are turned about

parts.note: Ed is a short form of the name Edward

explanation.surface: A cricketer named Edward makes a tricky run while England guard the Ashes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tricky' rearranges RUN to URN, then ED follows. The Ashes is the cricket trophy between England and Australia, kept in a tiny urn, which tempts a cricket reading of 'run'.
explanation.definitionFit: To put cremated remains into a funerary vessel is to look after them, here played on the cricket trophy's little vessel.

clue.text: He could make this geum blue

indicators.note: the clue says He could make this word into another, so the longer word less He leaves the answer

parts.note: the blue is a poetic term for the sky, the heavens
taken as written

explanation.surface: A gardener muses that a man could make his geum flower blue.
explanation.walkthrough: Turned round, 'He could make this ... blue' says HE plus the answer makes HEAVENS, the sky or 'the blue'; so HEAVENS without HE gives the plant.
explanation.definitionFit: Geum is the botanical genus of the plants known as herb bennet and water avens, so the name is a plant synonym.

clue.text: Troubleshooter extraordinary

parts.note: an official appointed to look into the public's complaints against government, a fixer of trouble outside the ordinary chain of authority, like an envoy extraordinary

explanation.surface: Praise for someone exceptionally good at sorting out problems.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extraordinary' looks like praise, but it is used as in 'ambassador extraordinary', for an official with a special commission.
explanation.definitionFit: A commissioner who investigates complaints against public bodies is in effect an appointed resolver of grievances.

clue.text: Tin or tape cutters

parts.note: a device that cuts open cans, or the dignitary who cuts the ribbon at a ceremony; both are said to open something

explanation.surface: A list of tools for cutting metal sheet or sticky tape.
explanation.walkthrough: Tin here is a can, which a gadget opens; the tape is the ribbon a celebrity snips to open a new building.
explanation.definitionFit: Those who cut ribbon declare a building open, and kitchen gadgets that cut cans also open them.

clue.text: The language of science is one thing; this is just the other

definitions.text: The language of science is one thing; this is just the other

parts.words: The language of science is one thing; this is just the other
parts.note: reverse the phrase and the science of language is the study of where words come from

explanation.surface: Contrasting scientific jargon with something else.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the nouns in 'the language of science' to get 'the science of language', in particular the study of word origins.
explanation.definitionFit: The study of word origins is a science of language, the converse of scientific language.

clue.text: To catch men she affects a pose

indicators.note: putting on a pose means the letters take up a different posture or arrangement

explanation.surface: A flirt strikes an attitude to attract men.
explanation.walkthrough: 'affects a pose' signals the anagram of MEN SHE; 'To catch' is the definition, though it reads as her motive.
explanation.definitionFit: To catch something in a net or tangle is to trap it, as fish are taken in mesh.

clue.text: Mr Bones's lolly?

parts.note: a skeleton nicknamed Mr Bones has no flesh, so a treat for him would be sweet flesh on the bones; lolly is a sweet

explanation.surface: Asking what sweet a man called Mr Bones likes.
explanation.walkthrough: Mr Bones is a skeleton, who would relish flesh; 'lolly' is a British word for a sweet, and the answer splits as sweet + meat.
explanation.definitionFit: A candied confection or sugary treat is called this, and the clue reads it as tasty flesh for a skeleton.

clue.text: Three quarters featured in a strange story in Salop

indicators.note: the compass points appear inside the jumbled letters
a strange version of a word has its letters turned oddly about

parts.note: south, west and east are three of the four quarters, or cardinal points, of the compass

explanation.surface: A tale of three local districts in an odd story from Shropshire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strange' rearranges STORY to OSTRY, and SWE, three compass points, goes after the O. Salop is an old name for Shropshire, an English county, where Oswestry is a market town.
explanation.definitionFit: This market town lies near the Welsh border in Shropshire, whose old name is Salop.

clue.text: The plea and the pleader

definitions.meaning: an earnest request or entreaty, as to God

explanation.definitionFit: The word means both an entreaty addressed to God and, read as pray plus -er, the person making that entreaty.

clue.text: The top of the radiator is hot — yes, red hot

indicators.note: only the top, the opening part, of the word is kept, its tail cut away

parts.note: taken as written
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on a tap

explanation.surface: A complaint that the radiator is scalding, very red hot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The top of' keeps RAD from radiator, then IS and H (hot) follow. A radish is red-skinned and peppery.
explanation.definitionFit: This salad root has red skin and a peppery bite, so it is both red and pungent.

clue.text: Still-water muses ?

parts.note: a pond is still water; as a verb the word means muses or thinks over

explanation.surface: A question about the goddesses of inspiration dwelling in a calm pool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'muses' looks like the nine goddesses, but it is a verb meaning thinks deeply; the 'still-water' reading splits the word into pond plus -ers.
explanation.definitionFit: To reflect carefully on something is to turn it over in the mind, exactly what someone musing does.

clue.text: Bird Shakespeare made much of after a drink

indicators.note: after places the drink before the other piece

parts.note: a pint is a measure of beer
Shakespeare's comedy Much Ado About Nothing made much ado

explanation.surface: Shakespeare made much of a bird after a few drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after' puts ADO, from Much Ado About Nothing, behind PINT. The pintado is the cape pigeon, a petrel.
explanation.definitionFit: The pintado petrel, or cape pigeon, is a seabird, so this is a species name.

clue.text: Billy the Kid in alliance with Tuck

definitions.text: Billy the Kid in alliance with Tuck

parts.words: Billy the Kid in alliance with Tuck
parts.note: a fat schoolboy called Billy in Frank Richards's Greyfriars stories is famously devoted to tuck, British school slang for sweets and cakes

explanation.surface: The Wild West outlaw teams up with Robin Hood's friar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Billy the Kid' and 'Tuck' suggest the outlaw and Friar Tuck, but Billy is the greedy schoolboy of the Greyfriars stories and tuck is school snacks.
explanation.definitionFit: The Owl of the Remove, a famously greedy fat schoolboy in British comic stories, is obsessed with snacks.

clue.text: Such were Lucy's ways

parts.note: Wordsworth's Lucy poem begins 'She dwelt among the ... ways', describing paths no one had walked

explanation.surface: A remark on a girl named Lucy's habits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ways' suggests habits, but Wordsworth's poem 'She dwelt among the untrodden ways' uses it for paths.
explanation.definitionFit: Paths nobody has walked on are unvisited, as were the remote ways where Wordsworth's Lucy lived.

clue.text: A card to flourish

definitions.meaning: a card of the suit that beats all others
to sound a trumpet, an old sense

explanation.definitionFit: A winning suit's card is called this, and in old usage the word also means to blow a fanfare.

clue.text: Balzac's cousin

parts.note: La Cousine ... is a novel by Balzac, its title character a poor relation

explanation.surface: A mention of a relative of the French novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cousin' is not Balzac's own relative but the title character of his novel La Cousine Bette.
explanation.definitionFit: The title of Balzac's novel names the cousin, a spinster poor relation seeking revenge on her family.

clue.text: But the note is uncommonly long

definitions.text: But the note is uncommonly long

parts.words: But the note is uncommonly long
parts.note: the name comes from Latin for short, yet in music it is the longest note, worth two ...

explanation.surface: A complaint that a written memo is far too long.
explanation.walkthrough: 'note' suggests a letter, but it is a musical note whose name means short, though it lasts twice a whole note.
explanation.definitionFit: This musical note lasts as long as two semibreves, though its Latin root means short.

clue.text: To see round the automation pioneers in Cornwall

indicators.note: one piece goes round, enclosing, the other

parts.note: taken as written
R.U.R., Karel Čapek's 1920 play Rossum's Universal Robots, introduced the word robot

explanation.surface: An instruction to go and see the automation pioneers somewhere in Cornwall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'see round' says TO goes round RUR, Čapek's robot play Rossum's Universal Robots. TRURO is the cathedral city of Cornwall, in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: This cathedral city is the county town of Cornwall, so the definition locates a place there.

clue.text: What the bank has to say of your financial affairs

definitions.text: What the bank has to say of your financial affairs

parts.words: What the bank has to say of your financial affairs
parts.note: the periodic account a bank sends its customers is called by a word that also means a pronouncement

explanation.surface: Wondering what one's bank thinks of one's money matters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has to say' makes the bank sound like a speaker, and the word also means a formal pronouncement.
explanation.definitionFit: A bank's periodic printout of credits and debits is also the word for a declaration, so the bank says something about your account.

clue.text: At par, yes, converted gives you your money back

indicators.note: converting money or a building alters its form, so the letters are changed round

explanation.surface: Bonds redeemed at their face value return your capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'converted' signals the anagram of PAR YES; 'At' only joins, though 'at par' reads as a finance phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: To pay back a loan or debt is to refund the lender's cash.

clue.text: A quorum of bewitching women attempt urban isolation

parts.note: a coven is a gathering of witches, traditionally thirteen
to try is to attempt

explanation.surface: Enough witches gather to try to cut a town off from the world.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'send someone to Coventry', a city in the English Midlands, is a British idiom for refusing to speak to them, hence 'urban isolation'.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom about this Midlands city means ostracising a person, so the city stands for being shunned.
